title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment that evaluated whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) changes the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) a guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), producing one LLM generation per task that was shared across arms (model_calls_used = 200; preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0). Observed (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0). Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that a verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this run. The paper’s principal outcome is methodological and artifact‑grounded: we (1) publish a complete preregistered paired run and analysis, (2) explain how generation semantics and task difficulty determine testability, and (3) provide concrete, archive‑grounded recommendations for reproducible repeats with independent per‑arm generation and stronger adversarial coverage.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) reduces operator workload but raises operational safety concerns: incorrect or ill‑timed network changes can break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior work advocates augmenting LLMs with deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, and generate–validate–repair loops to reduce constraint violations and hallucinations. We preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) to test whether a deterministic verifier pipeline reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts. The run is fully archived and machine‑readable: execution artifacts include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, and analysis outputs (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/paired_difference_figure.svg). The core scientific result observed here is negative in the sense that, under the executed generation semantics, the confirmatory test was non‑informative; this negative result yields specific methodological lessons about preregistration, generation semantics, model‑call budgeting, and adversarial task design that are broadly applicable to workflow‑centred NetOps evaluation.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototypes document growing LLM use in NetOps for intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis, and limited self‑healing; several works propose verifier‑in‑the‑loop and tool‑grounding to improve correctness and reduce hallucination risk [https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729, https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7132138, https://doi.org/10.1109/ojcoms.2026.3680457]. Generate–validate–repair and divide–verify–refine pipelines have been shown to reduce constraint violations in controlled settings, but effect sizes depend on verifier fidelity, generation semantics, and adversarial coverage. Red‑teaming and guardrail literature emphasize trade‑offs between safety and utility (false refusals) and recommend workflow‑centred, sandboxed evaluation; our experiment was designed to follow those prescriptions while providing a preregistered confirmatory test and reproducible artifact bundle.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand: The study preregistration (cand‑2026‑01‑prereg‑v1) defined the primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded minus baseline, SAFE encoded as 1) and froze a paired binary design with N=200 unique tasks. Sampling and task generation: a deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks under a fixed RNG seed. Task family and scope were limited to single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and three configuration fields (admin, mtu, vlan) per preregistration. Generation semantics and orchestration: the preregistration permitted either independent per‑arm generation or a shared_initial_candidate mode; the executed run used independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate semantics), so a single LLM candidate was generated per task and used for both baseline and guarded scoring. Model configuration and provider: the declared model was gpt‑5‑mini and the executed configuration is archived at execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"); execution accounting recorded model_calls_used = 200 while the preregistered maximum_model_calls was 400 (the latter would have covered independent per‑arm generation). Validator, scoring, and labels: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performed sandboxed deterministic intent/constraint validation under scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation. The validator returned a binary SAFE label (score = 1) or UNSAFE (score = 0) and detailed validator_traces (validation_before, validation_after, violation lists) which were archived per episode (execution/scoring/*.json). Analysis plan (frozen): paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency counts, exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value, and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Exclusions, missingness, and stopping rules: the preregistration defined deterministic duplicate detection and replacement policies; the execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, and zero exclusions, so the complete_pair_count used in the confirmatory analysis was 200. Reproducibility: all code, inputs, raw outputs, and analysis artifacts referenced above are archived in the supplied bundle and are referenced by artifact path in this manuscript.
sections.results: Confirmatory outcomes (reported for the adversarial cluster per preregistration): baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. The paired contingency table (SAFE encoding) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10000 resamples, seed = 1729; analysis artifacts archived). Execution accounting: planned episodes = 400 (200 tasks × 2 pipelines), completed_episode_count = 400, model_calls_used = 200, failed_episode_count = 0 (execution/execution_manifest.json). No verifier refusals, repairs, or discordant pairs occurred in the confirmatory dataset; repair_provider_trace entries in scoring JSONs are null for the sampled confirmatory episodes. Representative per‑task artifacts (execution/responses/task-0000XX-*.txt and execution/scoring/task-0000XX-*.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate content across baseline and guarded arms for every archived example we inspected, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate execution semantics.
sections.discussion: Methodological diagnosis: the combination of (A) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) and (B) the sampled tasks’ realized difficulty relative to gpt‑5‑mini produced identical per‑pair outputs that passed the deterministic validator; therefore the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, creating a ceiling effect. This outcome invalidated the preregistered power assumptions (which assumed baseline unsafe ≈10–15%) and rendered the planned McNemar test non‑informative for the causal question. Practical consequence: with identical per‑pair candidates, the verifier has no opportunity to reject or repair a baseline proposal because both arms share the same candidate. Artifact‑grounded recommendations for reproducible repeats (derived directly from the preregistration and execution manifest): (1) use independent per‑arm generation for paired causal tests so each pipeline receives distinct LLM outputs (this requires model_calls ≈ preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 for our N=200 design); (2) increase adversarial strength in prompt templates and include obfuscation transforms to elevate baseline error rates against the target LLM; (3) reserve a fraction of tasks for exploratory ROC/refusal diagnostics where the verifier is exercised with synthetic injected unsafe proposals; (4) consider multi‑model coverage to assess generality; (5) explicitly budget model_calls and record generation semantics in the preregistration to prevent unintentional shared‑candidate ceiling effects. Evidence‑to‑claim mapping: the claim that the confirmatory hypothesis was untestable in this run is supported by execution/model_configuration.json (generation semantics), execution/execution_manifest.json (model_calls_used = 200, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv (n11 = 200, SAFE rates = 1.0 for both arms), and representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/task-000001-*.json) that show shared_initial_candidate equality and validator traces with zero violations. Threats to validity: internal — the chosen generation semantics produced deterministic equivalence across arms; construct — synthetic tasks and validator scope may miss real NetOps failure modes; external — single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic topologies limit generality; conclusion validity — the observed null discordance prevents estimating a verifier causal effect in this run. Operational implication: a deterministic verifier remains a recommended safeguard in agentic NetOps workflows, but its empirical benefit requires experimental conditions that yield informative discordance (distinct per‑arm outputs and nonzero baseline error rates).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived, preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM baseline and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for gpt‑5‑mini, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; p = 1.0). Because identical per‑pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. The principal scientific contribution is methodological: preregistration choices (generation semantics, adversarial strength, and model‑call budgeting) determine whether a verifier effect is observable. We publish the complete archived bundle (execution/*, analysis/*, and scoring artifacts) and provide artifact‑grounded, actionable recommendations for reproducible repeats using independent per‑arm generation, stronger adversarial tasks, and model diversity.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in sandboxed synthetic states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
